justice: The lane is very narrow and most of the paved space is shared by pedestrians, small vehicles, and storefront spillover, so spatial resources are not clearly allocated among different road users.
A small shop canopy, stools, buckets, and goods placed along the right edge occupy part of the walking path, reducing fair access for passersby compared with the open center of the lane.
The brick-paved surface is generally level and there are no visible steps in the immediate foreground, which provides some baseline accessibility for general users.
No dedicated sidewalk, bike lane, or clearly marked pedestrian priority zone is visible, indicating limited equitable provision for different travel modes.
safety: The alley is narrow and appears to have low motor-vehicle speed, which can reduce severe crash risk for all road users.
A blue truck and several parked two-wheelers are visible ahead in the shared lane, creating potential conflicts and sightline narrowing in the already constrained corridor.
Storefront items and the large umbrella on the right intrude into the circulation space, increasing the chance of pedestrian-vehicle friction and walking detours.
Overhead utility wires are dense and visually chaotic, and lighting appears limited to sparse fixtures, which may reduce perceived safety, especially in lower-light conditions.
livability: The small street shop with drinks and daily goods supports everyday convenience and indicates local neighborhood service activity.
Visible people sitting and standing near the shop suggest some social interaction and street life rather than a fully inactive lane.
The lane is intimate in scale and directly connected to residential buildings, which can support neighborhood familiarity and local social contact.
However, the cramped right-side vending setup and vehicle presence reduce the amount of comfortable public space available for lingering.
sustainability: The compact alley form and mixed residential-commercial edge can support short local trips on foot rather than long-distance car dependence.
Several bicycles or electric two-wheelers are visible in the background, indicating some low-carbon mobility presence.
There is almost no visible street greenery, tree canopy, or planted area, limiting ecological and heat-mitigation benefits.
No visible stormwater features, permeable green strips, or other environmental infrastructure are present; the lane is dominated by hard paving and building walls.
aesthetics: The white walls and dark traditional rooflines create a relatively coherent architectural character along both sides of the alley.
The narrow stone-patterned paving and intimate lane width give the space a distinctive old-neighborhood atmosphere.
The storefront umbrella, exposed cookware, and overhead cables add visual clutter that weakens overall visual order.
Building facades appear somewhat worn but still maintain a recognizable vernacular identity, producing moderate rather than high aesthetic quality.
comfort: The large green shop umbrella provides localized shade near the storefront, offering some thermal relief in a small part of the lane.
There is no visible tree canopy or continuous shade structure along the alley, so thermal comfort is likely limited during hot weather.
The brick pavement appears relatively even and walkable, supporting basic physical comfort for short walking trips.
Path narrowing from shop goods, stools, and parked vehicles reduces physical and psychological comfort because users may need to negotiate space with others in close proximity.
walkability: The alley has a continuous paved surface and very short crossing distances because there are no wide carriageways, which supports basic walking movement.
Low-speed conditions are likely due to the narrow width, making the setting more walkable than a high-speed street.
There is no dedicated sidewalk separation, so pedestrians must share the same space with trucks, bikes, and storefront activity.
Obstructions from the shop umbrella, displayed items, and parked vehicles reduce effective walking width and continuity.
bikeability: The alley's low-speed environment can be somewhat compatible with cycling at very low volumes.
No dedicated bike lane, markings, or protected cycling space is visible, so cyclists must mix directly with pedestrians and occasional motor vehicles.
The narrow width and presence of a truck, parked two-wheelers, and shop encroachment make passing and maneuvering difficult for cyclists.
No bicycle parking facilities or cycling wayfinding are visible, indicating weak support for convenient everyday biking.
